question: Is it fair to be punished for all eternity for a finite number of sins?
asked: I'm having trouble understanding the issue of the eternality of Jahannam. How do we answer somebody who says that no matter how evil a person is, a finite amount of sins should not be punished for infinity?
answer:
So he asks a very deep and profound question of theology, and as you know, I always like to start with theology or methodology in my first question. So this is a two-part question. Number one, the wisdom of Jahannam being abad, abadiyyah, eternality. And number two, did Ibn Taymiyyah say that Jahannam is not eternal, that it will stop and that there will be no Jahannam after that?

As for the first question, realize that the scholars of Islam, of all of the firaq of Islam that are mainstream firaq, all of the classical groups of Islam, they have unanimously agreed that Jannah is eternal. No one of significance of any group denied that Jannah is eternal. And this is the standard position of all the schools of Islam.

As for Jahannam, then it is also the case that the majority position, the mainstream position of all of the groups, and even, of course, the one we're most interested in, Sunni Islam, is that Jahannam as well is eternal. And this is the standard doctrine that we find explicitly affirmed in many books of aqeedah, of many strands even of Sunnism, not just of any one particular strand.

And there are many evidences for this. For example, in the Qur'an, in Surah al-Jinn, Allah says:

> وَمَن يَعْصِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَإِنَّ لَهُ نَارَ جَهَنَّمَ خَالِدِينَ فِيهَا أَبَدًا

And by the way, FYI, three times in the Qur'an, three times exactly, Allah 'azza wa jall mentions "khalidina fiha abada" for Jahannam, and for Jannah it is more than this. For Jahannam, three times Allah says "khalidina fiha abada": they shall be residing in it forever. Khalid, and khalid actually does not mean forever. Khalid means long life; that's why the name Khalid is the one who lives long. So khulud does not necessarily mean forever. Khulud or khalid means long, but not forever. But the word abada, that's where we bring the twist, and we say abada means, and it does mean in Arabic, forever and ever and ever and ever. So three times Allah mentions Jahannam and then He says "khalidina fiha abada."

And in another verse: "Inna al-mujrimina fi 'adhabi jahannama khalidun." The sinners shall be in Jahannam. Sinners here means mushrikun, because whenever Allah says khalidin, then He's talking about the big sin, which is shirk. The sinners will be in Jahannam forever, a long time. It will never subside from them, and they shall remain in it. And We did not do injustice to them; they did injustice to themselves.

And there are many, many evidences in the Qur'an. For example: every time their skin withers away, We will give them another skin so that they can taste the torment. So there are many, many verses that indicate the eternality of Jahannam. Therefore it is pretty much standard doctrine that Jahannam will also last forever for the category of those who commit shirk. As for sinful Muslims, then by unanimous consensus they will not be in Jahannam forever. There's no controversy over that.

Now, the question was not over the eternality. The question was: how do we understand the wisdom? Because no matter how many sins a person has done, one lifetime is how long? 60 years, 70 years, 100 years. Let's even say the Prophet Nuh's time, 900 years. 900 years compared to the infinity of Jahannam. A kafir comes, a non-Muslim comes, or even a Muslim who has doubts, and says, "How is that fair?" This is the question, right? Okay, how do we respond to this question?

Firstly, realize that the problem of trying to explain the wisdom of Allah is an impossible one. You're asking a human to try to explain to you the wisdom of the creator of humans. It's not possible. And at the end of the day, perhaps our minds cannot understand. What are you going to do then? Rather than come with the assumption that I can understand every wisdom of Allah, this is an arrogant assumption. Who are you to understand every wisdom of Allah?

Now, is it wrong to ask for the wisdom? Is it wrong to ask the wisdom of a ruling? Yes or no? No. What's the evidence for this? How do we know it's okay to ask for the wisdom? Many: the sahabah asked; the angels asked, "Why are you creating Adam? Why would you put Adam?" It is not haram to try to ask why. It is haram to reject if you don't understand why. There's a difference between the two. "They ask you about this, they ask you about that." And no problem, ask. So the brother's question is not a problem. But before I answer, I want to say: even if you don't understand, or I don't understand, or I cannot help you understand, that doesn't change the ruling. So we have to answer the first in this manner.

Also realize that we fully believe that Allah does not do any injustice:

> إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَظْلِمُ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ
> وَمَا رَبُّكَ بِظَلَّامٍ لِّلْعَبِيدِ

Your Lord does not do dhulm. While we firmly believe this, what is dhulm? Dhulm is to burden someone with more than he or she can bear, or to punish someone for the sins of another person. This is dhulm. As for the severity of punishment, this is not dhulm. As for punishing this versus that, this is not dhulm.

The lawgiver in any law, in any land, in any constitution, they will give you the punishment. The same crime in this country: in 50 states you might have 50 different punishments. In this one country you might have 50. I'm exaggerating, but really I'm being true in some way. It is possible the same issue can have multiple punishments even in this land, depending on what state you live in. This is the reality of law: punishments are different. And Allah has every right to assign any punishment to any crime, because He is the lawgiver. He is the one who decides. So when He has assigned a punishment for a crime, this is not dhulm.

Dhulm would be to punish X for the crime of Y. That is dhulm, and Allah will never do that. These are two dhulms Allah said He will never do. As for the severity of punishment, there is no dhulm over here. The law is clear, and the law has been told to us. So there cannot be any dhulm for the quantity of punishment. At the end of the day, Allah is Malik, and He can punish as long as He wants for any crime that He has told us is a crime.

The second point here is that, to try to understand the wisdom, let us give some examples in our own human law. Do we judge the length of the sentence by the length of the crime or by the severity of the crime? Severity of the crime. A murder in our times, if you use a gun, will take one millisecond, 0.001 seconds, something like this. A murder will take less than one one-hundredth of a second, correct, if you use a gun. If somebody were to say, "Why was he given a lifetime for the deed that took 0.01?" will anybody think this is a logical i'tirad or excuse? Will anybody say, "Oh, the crime only took one second, why is he being punished for 70 years?" No. You don't look at how long the crime was; you look at how evil the crime was. Correct? This is the law everybody understands.

Now, in our religion, and honestly even without the Qur'an telling us this, common sense tells us the biggest crime of any human being is to ignore why he has been created. What bigger crime is there than to ignore, to not even think about, to simply turn away from the highest purpose of existence, which is to really try to find out: Why am I here? Who created me? What's the purpose of life? Worship of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. And therefore it is completely logical and rational that the one who refused to even think about Allah, the real mushrik and kafir —

And that's why we say the believers who are sinful, this does not apply to them. The believers who believe in Allah, who have an ounce of iman, as the Prophet ﷺ said, eventually they'll be moved from Jahannam. No problem there. That is where the logic applies: okay, a finite quantity of sins, yes. But the one who did not even think about sin and good, he didn't think about heaven and hell, life and death, he never thought about why he is here, then this person, subhanAllah, what was his life for? What did he do with all of his life?

As Aisha said about her great-uncle Ibn Jud'an: "Ya Rasulullah, Ibn Jud'an did so much good. Would Allah forgive him?" And the Prophet ﷺ said, "No, because Ibn Jud'an never once said, 'O Allah, forgive me.'" He never once, even as a mushrik, as a pagan, as a kafir, he never said, "O Allah, forgive me." Allah was never on his mind. Why should then Allah turn to him and forgive him?

So the one who never thinks of Allah, turns away from Allah, has no purpose other than to live like an animal, when Allah made you a human and better than an animal, and you live your life like an animal, then **the severity of the punishment is based upon the severity of the crime**. And what greater crime is there than to turn away from Allah?

And this is indicated in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, an authentic hadith. The Prophet ﷺ says that Allah will say to the one who is being punished the least in Jahannam, the least, ya'ni a mushrik who is punished forever, Allah will say, "O so-and-so, would you give up all that you possessed in your life, your wealth, your family, everything? Would you give it up right now to be safe from Jahannam?" And the man will say, "Yes, I will, and ten times more." Allah will say (listen to this), "But I didn't ask you for all of this on this earth. I only asked that you worship Me and don't do shirk with Me. And you refused. You refused, and you insisted on worshipping other than Me."

So here we have one of the wisdoms of the eternality of the punishment. What did Allah ask of us? All of our time, all of our wealth? No. Allah said: understand who created you, and believe in that entity, and worship Him. And if you're sinful, turn to Him for forgiveness; Allah is Ghafur and Rahim. But the one who didn't even care to think…

And that's why, again, we go back to another question I gave many, many months ago, about non-Muslims who never heard of Islam. And I mentioned: look, we say Islam is the only way to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. There's one path. But there might be people on other paths. The path does not lead to Jannah, but Allah knows the person was sincere, not the path, and Allah might forgive the person, not the path. So we firmly believe somebody who tried to be religious in an environment where there was no Islam, who tried to be sincere, righteous, pious in his own way, without knowing Islam and whatnot, inshallah, this person, we hope the best for him. We don't pronounce a verdict in this dunya, but in the akhirah we hope the best for him. No problem with that person. But how about the one who just did not care? "The one who turned away from Allah's dhikr." So the severity of the punishment is due to the severity of the crime.

The third thing we can say here is another thing that some of our scholars have mentioned: the eternality of the punishment is due to the fact that the crime would have been eternal if they lived eternally. In other words, Allah says in the Qur'an they want to come back to this earth, right? And Allah says, "If they were to be returned, they would go back to what they were doing." This is a very key phrase in the Qur'an. Allah says: if I were to bring them back, they would go back to doing what they had been doing. Which means if they live forever, their shirk would be forever, and so their punishment is forever as well.

So these are three answers that can be given to respond to the wisdom.
